Photograph: c/o Rebecca Howard View image in fullscreen ‘You don’t often see a dead tree in a painting’: Rebecca Howard working on one of her canvases. Photograph: c/o Rebecca Howard Rewilding Artist delights in beautiful ‘mess’ and dead trees of England’s rewilding sites Rebecca Howard spent two years visiting projects and painting landscapes that feature in West Sussex exhibition Patrick Barkham Sat 12 Sep 2026 01.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Rewilding areas do not usually conform to traditional notions of beauty in England’s green and pleasant land. Detractors may bewail the beaver-felled trees, untidy scrub, deadwood, weeds, mud and “mess”. But a new exhibition highlights the aesthetic delights that can be discovered on rewilding sites where fungi grows on dying trees, water buffalo gather in new wetlands and brown-watered beaver pools flood once-desiccated fields. The artist Rebecca Howard devoted two years to visiting rewilding projects across England before spending a month painting each of nine large canvases that reveal what happens when people step back from intensive management of land and allow wild nature to take a leading role. View image in fullscreen A beaver on the rewilded Knepp estate. Photograph: Charlie Burrell/PA “I wanted to create a positive exhibition that people could view and feel empowered to do something of their own, and not feel totally overwhelmed by the challenges we face with our climate and biodiversity crisis,” said Howard. “If you walk into an art gallery you’re faced with seascapes or bluebell woods but you don’t often see a dead tree in a painting.” View image in fullscreen Cabilla Tor at Sunrise by Rebecca Howard. Photograph: Rob Percy/Rebecca Howard Howard, whose exhibition opens at rewilded Knepp, West Sussex, on 12 September, began by visiting Cabilla, a fragment of Cornish temperate rainforest which is being restored and extended by the Thousand Year Trust charity founded by Merlin Hanbury-Tenison. Over the following months, Howard explored renowned rewilding sites including the pioneering Knepp estate , which began the British rewilding movement, and the Devon farm turned back to nature by the outspoken rewilder Derek Gow , who has also overseen the reintroduction of beavers, storks and water voles to many sites across Britain. But Howard was also invited into less widely known projects including, in Derby, the largest urban rewilding project in Britain , and Broughton Sanctuary, a North Yorkshire estate owned by the same family for more than 900 years that is taking a land-healing turn in the 21st century. At all the sites she ended up painting, Howard discovered new kinds of land management and beauty that challenge conventional notions and customs. At Hamatethy Farm , a rewilded hill farm in Cornwall, she found a huge beach tree that had most of its trunk chewed by resident beavers but was still standing. “It was a felled tree waiting to happen but there was something very beautiful about that stasis between a living and a dead tree,” she said. “You know it’s going to crash down at some point but it’s going to provide so much habitat when it does and it’s actually a beautiful object in the way it’s been gnawed. It’s exciting. I’m definitely on the side of seeing beauty in new ways.” Howard, who chose the sites for their varied habitat, with each one also being a member of the Rewilding Britain charity’s network, was struck by the mix of private and charity landowners’ openness to change and openness to visitors like herself. View image in fullscreen Allestree Park in Derbyshire. Photograph: Eclicktique Photography/Alamy “Each of the sites were after the same thing – they wanted to increase the biodiversity of their place and get the most out of their land – but they were also all so keen to show me around. They came back to me with enthusiasm and openness, there was no agenda,” she said. “Walking around with them, there was this excitement – some had only been doing it for five years and already there was so much positive change: the coming back of lost species and the constant unknown quality to it, which might be a bit disconcerting to a lot of us.” At Knepp, Howard studied the standing deadwood, a vital habitat for hundreds of invertebrates but one which has not been tolerated in recent centuries because dead trees have been cut down and tidied away, or more recently removed over health and safety fears. View image in fullscreen Being a Beaver by Rebecca Howard. Photograph: Rob Percy/Rebecca Howard At Moor Barton in Devon, she joined a group ring-barking non-native larch trees. “There was a sense of, ‘What are we doing killing things?’, but what we were doing was creating deadwood and removing these massive, fast-growing trees that were crowding out young oaks and birches. Give it a year and it will really benefit that land,” she said. Each canvas is 120cm tall and 70cm wide. “When you’re standing in front of them they take up your whole vision. The idea is that you’re transported to that place and you get some sense of what it’s like to visit,” said Howard, who hopes the exhibition, which runs until 18 October at Knepp, will then tour other places in Britain. Lia Brazier, the creative director at Knepp, said: “Rewilding needs to exist not only in our landscapes, but in our culture and imagination too, so we’re thrilled to be hosting this important body of work. Rebecca’s paintings offer a new way of seeing these changing landscapes, revealing the extraordinary diversity and abundance that can emerge when nature is given space to recover. We hope this work will inspire people to connect more deeply with nature and see the possibility of a wilder future as something not only tangible, but essential.” Howard said art had a lovely way of drawing people in and that she “wanted to show the beauty of rewilding. I don’t have any land myself but as an artist I can raise awareness of the benefits of rewilding. It’s my gift to their cause.” Explore more on these topics Rewilding Art Painting England Exhibitions Wildlife West Sussex news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Environment Climate crisis Wildlife Energy Pollution Green light

(AP Photo/Kateryna Klochko) Correction: Byline corrected to Kateryna Klochko, instead of Evgeniy Maloletka KYIV – Russian drones struck the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia on Monday, a day after Kyiv’s forces fired more than 1,000 drones at Russia, officials said. The relentless daily attacks underscore the lack of significant progress in diplomatic efforts to end the fighting more than four years after Russia invaded its neighbor . Recommended Videos There is no sign the war is abating as world leaders gather this week at the U.N. General Assembly. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he expects to meet with U.S. President Donald Trump at the annual event in New York. Russian President Vladimir Putin is not due to attend. Trump on Monday called the war “ridiculous” and said Moscow had “unfortunately lost control” of its diesel oil production as Ukraine targets Russian refineries with long-range drones. “A large number of (Russian) diesel refineries have been blown up and are, at least temporarily, out of commission,” he said in a social media post. Earlier this month, Trump urged Zelenskyy to halt the refinery strikes , saying the attacks are causing a global shortage and price spikes. Zelenskyy responded to Trump in a post on X, noting that Kyiv has offered “dozens of diplomatic proposals on how to end this war with dignity, guarantee security, and prevent new Russian invasions.” “Ukraine’s energy sector, critical infrastructure, and our food exports must stop being targets for Russia, and this will lead to matching de-escalation steps on our part,” he said. European leaders, fearing Moscow has malicious intentions on their continent, are keen to put further pressure on Putin to withdraw from Ukraine, but the Russian leader has given no indication he is ready to give up his goals . Russia hits apartment blocks and a shopping mall, officials say The Russian bombardment of Zaporizhzhia late Sunday hit apartment blocks, a university and a shopping mall, among other sites, and wounded five people, Zelenskyy said on social media Monday. Russia also struck nine other regions of Ukraine, he said. A Russian drone struck a home in northeastern Ukraine’s Kharkiv region on Monday, killing a 45-year-old woman and seriously injuring her 13-year-old son, according to Ukraine’s State Emergency Service. “Russia is not backing down from its escalation and is sending many signals that it is ready to expand the war,” Zelenskyy said. “At the U.N. General Assembly, we will discuss how we can achieve peace through joint efforts.” The Russian military overnight targeted Ukrainian logistics hubs, warehouses and ports, among other military-related sites, the Russian Defense Ministry said in a statement Monday. The attacks came after Ukraine launched a huge swarm of drones at Russia from Saturday to Sunday, including hundreds aimed at Moscow, as voters turned out for the third and last day of a carefully orchestrated parliamentary election . The Russian Defense Ministry said Monday that its air defenses overnight downed 244 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions and the waters of the Black Sea. Meanwhile, Ukraine’s air force said Monday it shot down or suppressed 148 Russian drones in an overnight attack. Moldova reports another drone incursion During the aerial barrages, drones have repeatedly strayed into neighboring countries, unnerving leaders who are wary of Russia and fear being dragged into conflict. Moldova’s Ministry of Defense said Monday that part of the country's airspace in the north was temporarily closed overnight after surveillance systems detected an “aerial object” entering its national airspace shortly after midnight. In recent weeks, Moldova’s airspace has been violated multiple times, and drone debris has been found on its territory. With electronic jamming knocking drones off course, it was not clear whether the drones were Russian or Ukrainian, though officials have often singled out Moscow for blame. Moldova’s pro-Western President Maia Sandu has repeatedly condemned Russia for its war on Ukraine, and earlier this month said Moscow’s “brutal war is reaching our border” following Russian strikes along Moldova’s frontier with Ukraine. Drone incursions into Romania’s airspace have also increased significantly. ___ AP reporters Stephen McGrath in Leamington Spa, England, and Seun Min Kim in Washington contributed to this story. ___ Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. https://www.dw.com/en/us-sanctions-targe.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OKm5 In Iran, rail transport has become important for moving goods as businesses contend with sanctions, regional tensions and disruptions to trade routes Image: Rouzbeh Fouladi/ZUMA/IMAGO Advertisement The United States has opened another front in its economic pressure campaign against Iran , this time targeting the railways Tehran increasingly relies on as maritime trade becomes more difficult. On October 1, the US Treasury sanctioned three Iranian railway companies alongside seven automakers and five foreign suppliers of automotive parts as part of its Operation Economic Outcast. Washington says Iran's rail and automotive industries provide revenue and logistical capacity to the state and are connected to networks involving the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) . The timing of the move is significant. Since the US maritime blockade sharply restricted Iran's southern trade routes, Tehran has tried to move more goods through its land borders and railway connections with China, Central Asia, Russia and Turkey. Rail transport has become more important just as Washington decided to target it. Iran expands regional rail links Shahriar Naghizadeh, director general for foreign trade at Iran's railway authority, was quoted by the semi-official Mehr news agency as saying that the country has around 15,000 kilometers (9,300 miles) of main and secondary railway lines, more than 35,000 wagons and nearly 500 diesel locomotives. The network carried around 44 million tons of freight in the Iranian year ending in March 2026, up from about 40 million tons the previous year, according to Naghizadeh. And authorities are targeting 54 million tons this year. Can Trump’s diesel deal bring down US fuel prices? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Iran is linked to neighboring markets through 13 rail crossings, providing overland access to Turkey, Azerbaijan, Afghanistan, Pakistan and onward routes to Central Asia and China via Turkmenistan. The new US sanctions raise questions about how foreign railway operators, freight forwarders, banks and insurers will continue dealing with Iranian rail companies. China-Iran rail traffic expands Bloomberg reported in May that freight trains traveling from the Chinese city of Xi'an to Tehran had increased from around one per week before the US blockade to roughly one every three or four days. In September, a train left China carrying automotive parts, consumer goods and other cargo. It ran through Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan before entering Iran at Sarakhs with an expected transit time of 14 to 16 days. For Iran, such services offer a route to Chinese suppliers that avoids the area around the Strait of Hormuz . But advertised transit times do not necessarily reflect what an importer experiences. Ships wanting to transit the Strait of Hormuz have faced recurring and serious disruptions since the start of the US-Iran war earlier this year Image: Amirhosein Khorgooi/ISNA/AP Photo/picture alliance Delivery date cannot be guaranteed A Chinese freight company told DW that actual delivery times can stretch far beyond advertised schedules because of border inspections, customs procedures and train availability. It estimated that rail transit along the main route from western China to Tehran would take 50-60 days under current conditions. Road transport along a similar route is around 22 to 25 days. The gap between a scheduled 14-day transit time and commercial estimates of up to 60 days highlights one of the central challenges facing Iran. Customs inspections, gauge changes, payment problems and sanctions can all be another potential point of delay. Increasing the number of trains also requires more locomotives, wagons and cooperation from several transit countries. Rail works best for critical inputs Alireza Salavati, managing director of London-based Middle East Analytica, said rail is increasingly useful for Iran but should not be mistaken as a replacement for maritime trade. "A workable overland route now links China and Iran, but I would not call it a replacement for sea freight," he told DW. Under normal conditions, ships can move far larger quantities at lower unit costs. Rail becomes more attractive for goods where speed and continuity matter more than the cheapest transport. That includes automotive components, machinery, electronics and industrial inputs, whose absence can stop an entire production line. US military buildup: What message is it sending Iran? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video When delays become a cash problem Salavati argues that the effect on companies cannot be measured only in freight charges. For a manufacturer importing $1 million (€890,000) worth of inputs every 30 days, a 30-day journey means roughly a million dollars of inventory may be tied up in transit. Cutting the journey to 15 days could reduce that amount significantly, depending on payment arrangements. The reverse can be much more damaging. If input costs rise while delivery times stretch from 30 to 45 days, companies need more working capital simply to maintain the same production flow, the expert explained, pointing out that a factory can have customers and orders but still have to reduce production because too much cash is trapped in goods that have not arrived. "Reliability matters as much as speed," Salavati said. "A 15-day train is little use if the container waits a week to depart, or if the bank or insurer will not touch it." The new US sanctions add another source of uncertainty to that calculation. Sanctions push trade toward other corridors Optimizing its railway use would give Iran more options than having to rely on southern ports alone, but the overall scale remains limited. Washington's sanction strategy is designed to isolate Iran by closing maritime, financial, aviation and now railway channels. Still, Salavati argues that the same pressure may accelerate Iran's integration with alternative networks. "Washington's efforts to isolate Iran may also be pushing it deeper than at any point in recent years into China's economic orbit and closer to Russia's wartime strategic system," he said. That does not mean China or Russia can make up for the economic cost of US pressure, since Iranian importers still need insurers, banks and customers able to absorb higher prices. Container trains can only carry a fraction of what a large cargo vessel can transport, so for now, rail provides Iran with a limited alternative trade channel . Its wider success depends on better financing and becoming more reliable — but even then it is not a wholesale substitute for sea freight. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Demonstrators gather in Paris as fresh protests sweep France France Hundreds of thousands march across France in protests over schools and policing Government estimates at least 400,000 people took part, but trade unions say the number is double that Angelique Chrisafis in Paris Sat 24 Oct 2026 13.54 EDT Last modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 15.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday in largely peaceful protests to support schoolchildren’s demands for more teachers and repairs to dilapidated buildings, as Emmanuel Macron faces a social and political crisis in his final months as president. In Paris, at least 110,000 people marched along the eastern edge of the city, according to government estimates. They supported high schoolers but also complained of the high cost of living and the government’s heavy policing, saying riot police had been sent to target school protesters over the past month, instead of the government offering political solutions. The mood in Paris on Saturday afternoon was peaceful and lighthearted, with brass bands playing and children and grandchildren present. Some people carried banners critical of the government’s policing, saying: “Oppression breeds rebellion” and “The right to protest”. But at the end of the Paris demonstration, at Porte de Vincennes on the city’s eastern edge, different groups of masked men dressed in black emerged who had not appeared to have taken part in the peaceful march. Some groups of masked men threw glass bottles and stones at police, who responded with teargas, water cannon and stun grenades. A bin was set alight and fireworks were set off towards police. Major protests in Paris and other French cities in challenge to Macron – in pictures Read more Police also fired teargas to prevent protesters in Lyon, Lille, Montpellier, Nantes and Toulouse from reaching city centres. In Marseille, some bin fires were lit amid clashes with police. The government estimated that at least 400,000 people had marched across France . Trade unions estimated the number at double that. The interior ministry said there had been almost 1,000 arrests. More than 70,000 police were on the streets of French cities, with shops boarded up and many museums closed. The government had feared a repeat of last Saturday, when, despite peaceful protests taking place, France saw one of the most violent days of unrest in years with public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted and at least 2,700 people arrested in cities across the country. At Saturday’s protests, there was widespread anger at Macron for banning non-union demonstrations that his government deemed “illegitimate” and for keeping all protesters away from city centres. View image in fullscreen At the end of the Paris demonstration, different groups of masked men dressed in black emerged and threw glass bottles and stones at police. Photograph: Thibault Camus/AP At the Paris march, Nadège, a 43-year-old communications worker, said she had been teargassed last weekend at a peaceful demonstration. “I’m out again peacefully today to support everyone who is brave enough to demonstrate. It does take courage. People are afraid now. We have to keep our rights alive … In France, it’s our legal right to protest in the street and I’m here to defend that.” A 21-year-old student from a Paris science faculty that is now blockaded by demonstrators said: “We feel in France that we are increasingly living in an authoritarian regime that is trying to stop our democratic right to protest in the street.” The government has been facing a crisis since the start of high school demonstrations in mid-September, when children aged between 15 and 18 began protesting against staff shortages at their schools, leaking and crumbling buildings, and a lack of chairs in overcrowded classrooms. It grew into the biggest youth movement in years, with trade unions, teachers and parents joining. Police investigations are under way after some children and protesters were maimed and injured by explosive police weaponry. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion At Saturday’s march there were some people dressed in yellow vests who had taken part in the gilets jaunes anti-government protests of 2018 and 2019. Standing amid demonstrators, Jérôme Rodrigues, a key figure from the gilets jaunes protest, said: “Today the government is afraid; that is why they are pushing demonstrators to the edge of the city, away from places of power. It’s not police shields that will provide an answer to French people struggling and unable to make ends meet.” He said it was likely that demonstrations would continue each weekend. NFL shutters Paris fan experience as protests overshadow first France game Read more Pierre, 60, a retired banking consultant, said he was demonstrating in support of school students. “I have an eight-year-old granddaughter. I want her to have a brighter future than the sombre times we are facing today. There is a complete refusal by the government to listen to people’s demands.” Jesse, 40, a charity worker from the north of Paris, carrying a sign saying “Free Hugs”, said: “I’m so angry. I’m here to support schoolchildren’s demands for better conditions. I’m so proud of them and we have to stand together.” She said: “I know I’m not going to war by coming out to demonstrate peacefully. But at times it really does feel like a war … This is the first time I’ve prepared so carefully for a peaceful march, wearing old clothes in case they are gassed or torn.” In Orléans, thousands of people shouting anti-fascist slogans marched against a congress being held by Marine Le Pen’s far-right anti-immigration the National Rally party. Protesters criticised Le Pen, who is a frontrunner in next year’s presidential election, as well as Macron, who steps down from power next year. “Macron, resign. Le Pen in prison,” the crowd shouted.
